screens.title: EtherChannel: Link Aggregation for Bandwidth and Resilience
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore EtherChannel, also called link aggregation. EtherChannel lets you treat multiple physical Ethernet links as a single logical interface, giving you higher aggregated bandwidth and built-in redundancy. For example, four 1‑gigabit links can form one 4‑gigabit port-channel so traffic can use more capacity while surviving a single link failure. We will cover the negotiation protocols you can use, how to configure an EtherChannel on Cisco Catalyst switches, how to select load balancing that matches your traffic patterns, and how to verify and troubleshoot a bundle. You will also practice a two‑switch lab that uses four links with LACP and a trunk carrying VLANs 10, 20, and 30. Understanding when to use static versus dynamic aggregation, and why interface parameters must match, avoids the most common formation failures. By the end you should be able to build, verify, and tune EtherChannels to improve resilience and utilization in an enterprise fabric. Consider how combining links changes failure modes and capacity planning in your own network.

screens.title: What is EtherChannel?
screens.narratorSegment: EtherChannel is a method of bundling multiple physical Ethernet links into one logical interface. This logical interface is often named a Port-channel. The primary benefits are twofold. First, aggregate bandwidth: several 1‑gigabit links appear as a single higher‑capacity link, which increases throughput without requiring changes to upper-layer protocols. Second, link redundancy: if a single physical member fails, the port-channel remains operational using the remaining members, providing graceful degradation rather than a hard outage. A concrete example is connecting two switches with four GigabitEthernet links. When bundled, the pair behaves like one 4‑gigabit link. Traffic distribution across the members depends on the switch's hashing algorithm. A common misconception is that EtherChannel balances every flow evenly; in reality, the hashing algorithm maps flows to member links, so some flows remain on a single physical member. That is why choosing the right load‑balancing key matters. Remember that the port-channel is the object you configure for trunks, allowed VLANs, and Layer 2/3 settings; member interfaces are assigned to the channel-group and inherit the port-channel configuration implicitly. Consider how bundling affects failure domains and capacity planning before deployment.

keyIdea.text: EtherChannel bundles links into a Port-channel to combine capacity and provide resilience without changing logical addressing.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is EtherChannel?
Bundle physical Ethernet links into a single logical Port-channel for higher throughput and link-level redundancy.
Benefits
  • Aggregate bandwidth from multiple physical links.
  • Seamless redundancy if a member link fails.
  • Apply trunk and VLAN settings at the port-channel level.
Concrete example
Four GigabitEthernet links between two switches combined into interface Port-channel1 yields an aggregated 4 Gbps logical link, with traffic distribution determined by the configured load‑balancing algorithm.
Common misconception

EtherChannel does not split a single TCP flow across multiple links. It distributes flows based on hashes, so per‑flow throughput remains bounded by a single member link.

Port-channel1

[Multiple member links aggregate into Port-channel]
Key Takeaway

Think of EtherChannel as parallel lanes on a highway; total capacity rises, but a single vehicle (flow) stays in one lane based on hashing rules.

screens.title: PAgP versus LACP
screens.narratorSegment: There are two main dynamic negotiation protocols for EtherChannel on Cisco gear: PAgP and LACP. PAgP is Cisco‑proprietary and uses modes named desirable and auto. Desirable actively tries to form an EtherChannel, while auto waits to be contacted. LACP is an open standard (IEEE 802.3ad) and uses active and passive modes that behave similarly: active initiates negotiation and passive waits. For either protocol, one side must actively initiate for the bundle to form. A common mistake is setting both sides to the passive equivalent—auto on PAgP or passive on LACP—which prevents negotiation and leaves member interfaces unbundled. LACP is preferred in mixed‑vendor environments because it is standard, and it provides richer fault detection and negotiation. A static or forced EtherChannel using on mode bypasses negotiation altogether; this can work but removes dynamic checks and makes the setup fragile to mismatch. In practice choose LACP for interoperability and operational visibility, avoid static on in production unless you have a controlled environment, and always confirm mode pairings when a bundle fails to form. PAgP versus LACP means lacp is the open standard preferred for interoperability; pagp is cisco proprietary. mode pairing must include an active/desirable side to form a channel.. In practical terms, protocol differences, modes, and practical implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison
PAgP vs LACP
Understand modes, vendor scope, and recommended uses.
PAgP (Cisco)
Modes: desirable (active) and auto (passive). Cisco proprietary; valid when both ends run PAgP.
LACP (Standard)
Modes: active (active) and passive (passive). Open standard, preferred for multi-vendor interoperability and better diagnostics.
Static 'on' mode
Forces an EtherChannel without negotiation. Simpler but lacks protocol checks and is more vulnerable to misconfiguration.
Mode pairing reference
PAgP: desirable + auto or desirable + desirable forms channel. auto + auto will not form.
LACP: active + passive or active + active forms channel. passive + passive will not form.
Static: on forces the bundle regardless of remote mode but offers no negotiation safety.
Pro Tip

Use LACP in production except when both endpoints are controlled Cisco devices and you need a deliberately simple static bundle for specific use cases.

screens.title: Configuring an EtherChannel
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring EtherChannel on Cisco Catalyst switches follows a predictable sequence. First, ensure all physical interfaces you will bundle share the same fundamental settings: speed, duplex, native VLAN, trunk encapsulation, allowed VLAN list for trunks, and Layer 2 or Layer 3 mode. Mismatches in any of those commonly prevent the bundle from forming. Next, create or use a port-channel logical interface and apply the shared configuration there. Then, assign member interfaces to the channel-group with a number and mode. For example, using LACP active mode, you run interface range GigabitEthernet1/0/1 - 4 and then channel-group 1 mode active. After grouping, the port-channel interface should reflect the common configuration. If you are creating a trunk EtherChannel, apply switchport mode trunk and switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30 on interface Port-channel1. Finally, bring interfaces up with no shutdown. A typical error is applying allowed VLANs only to physical member ports but not to the port-channel; always apply the operational settings to the port-channel itself. Follow this sequence during configuration and verify at each step with the show commands to catch mismatches early. Configuring an EtherChannel means make member interfaces identical, apply common settings to the port-channel, then assign members with channel-group mode.. In practical terms, step-by-step commands and interface requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow
How to configure an EtherChannel
Follow a checklist to avoid common mismatches that prevent bundle formation.
1
Match interface parameters
Speed, duplex, native VLAN, trunk allowed lists, and operational mode must be identical across members.
2
Create Port-channel and apply config
Configure switchport mode, trunk allowed VLANs, or IP addressing on interface Port-channelX.
3
Assign member interfaces
Use interface range and channel-group <number> mode <mode> to bind physical ports to the port-channel.
4
Verify and bring up
Use show etherchannel summary and show interfaces port-channel to confirm operational status.
Checklist
  • Speed and duplex identical on members.
  • Same native VLAN and trunk allowed VLAN list.
  • Layer 2 or Layer 3 mode consistent.
  • Correct channel-group number on both ends.
Example commands
configure terminal
interface range GigabitEthernet1/0/1 - 4
 channel-group 1 mode active
 no shutdown
!
interface Port-channel1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
 no shutdown
!
port-channel load-balance src-dst-ip
!
end

screens.title: Load Balancing Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: EtherChannel load balancing decides which physical member carries a given flow. Different switches support options that use MAC addresses, IP addresses, or transport ports as hashing keys. Common options include src-mac, dst-mac, src-dst-mac, src-ip, dst-ip, src-dst-ip, and port-based keys like src-port or src-dst-port for Layer 4 awareness. The hashing function combines the selected fields to produce an index that maps to a member link. The practical impact is significant. For example, if a single server sends many flows to many clients and you use src-mac, all flows from that server will hash the same and congest one link. In this scenario, src-dst-ip or src-dst-port spreads flows across members better. When choosing an algorithm, analyze whether many-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many, or large single flows dominate your traffic. Test with representative traffic and monitor per-link utilization. A common misconception is that more links always equal balanced usage; only an appropriate hashing key produces balanced outcomes for your traffic mix. Load Balancing Algorithms means select hashing keys that reflect your traffic patterns; src-dst-ip or src-dst-port often improves distribution for many-to-one traffic.. In practical terms, how hashing choices affect traffic distribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Load Balancing Algorithms
Choose the hashing fields that will produce even link utilization given your traffic patterns.
Common options
  • src-mac, dst-mac, src-dst-mac
  • src-ip, dst-ip, src-dst-ip
  • src-port, dst-port, src-dst-port (Layer 4 aware)
Example

A single server talking to many clients will likely overload src-mac hashing. Changing to src-dst-ip or src-dst-port creates finer granularity and spreads flows across links.

Visual: hashing examples
src-mac: good for many sources to many destinations, poor for one source to many destinations.
src-dst-ip: often best when a few servers talk to many clients because both endpoints vary the hash.
src-dst-port: best when many connections exist between the same hosts using different ports.
Why it matters

Choosing the wrong algorithm can leave some physical links idle while others saturate. Tune based on observed flow patterns.

screens.title: Static 'on' Mode and Its Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Static EtherChannel, configured with the on mode, forces member interfaces to behave as a bundle without any negotiation protocol. This can be useful in tightly controlled, vendor-homogeneous environments where you want to avoid protocol overhead. However, it removes the dynamic safeguards that PAgP or LACP provide. There is no negotiation to agree on matching parameters, and no protocol timers or link failure reports are exchanged. That means a single‑sided misconfiguration or a missing member on the remote side can create asymmetric link behavior or forwarding anomalies. For example, if one end has channels assigned but the other end does not, traffic may be blackholed or looped depending on spanning-tree and interface states. Therefore in production you should default to LACP for interoperability and operational visibility, and only use on mode when you control both endpoints and accept the operational risk. When you do use static on, test failure scenarios and verify member interfaces remain synchronized under link flaps. Static 'on' Mode and Its Trade-offs means on mode forces aggregation but lacks negotiation and fault detection; prefer lacp for production resilience and visibility.. In practical terms, when to use forced port-channel and what you lose. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition
Static 'on' EtherChannel
Forces interfaces into a port-channel without negotiation. Simpler but less safe.
Trade-offs

Common mistake

Using on mode in a multi-vendor or mixed-configuration environment often leads to unexpected behavior. Reserve it for controlled cases only.

When to consider 'on'
When both endpoints are Cisco, consistently configured, and you need a simple forced bundle for a lab or a constrained production case.
Key Takeaway

Static on gives simplicity at the cost of operational safeguards. Prefer LACP when reliability matters.

In this lesson we explore EtherChannel, also called link aggregation. EtherChannel lets you treat multiple physical Ethernet links as a single logical interface, giving you higher aggregated bandwidth and built-in redundancy. For example, four 1‑gigabit links can form one 4‑gigabit port-channel so traffic can use more capacity while surviving a single link failure. We will cover the negotiation protocols you can use, how to configure an EtherChannel on Cisco Catalyst switches, how to select load balancing that matches your traffic patterns, and how to verify and troubleshoot a bundle. You will also practice a two‑switch lab that uses four links with LACP and a trunk carrying VLANs 10, 20, and 30. Understanding when to use static versus dynamic aggregation, and why interface parameters must match, avoids the most common formation failures. By the end you should be able to build, verify, and tune EtherChannels to improve resilience and utilization in an enterprise fabric. Consider how combining links changes failure modes and capacity planning in your own network.

By the end of this chapter you will explain why EtherChannel is used and how it improves capacity and availability in enterprise links. You will distinguish PAgP and LACP, including the valid negotiation mode pairings that allow a bundle to form. You will configure a multi‑link EtherChannel on Cisco Catalyst switches, apply trunking and allowed VLAN lists to the port-channel, and set the global load‑balancing algorithm to meet traffic patterns. Finally, you will verify operation using the show commands and troubleshoot common formation failures caused by mismatched interface parameters. Each objective focuses on practical skill: explanation builds conceptual clarity, differentiation helps you choose protocols, configuration gives you hands‑on commands, and load‑balancing tuning ensures even utilization. A short example is included for each objective so you can picture the task: explain bundling using a 4x1G example, compare desirable/auto with active/passive, configure interface range channel-group commands, and choose src-dst-ip when one server talks to many clients. These objectives map directly to lab steps and verification tasks you will practice.

This lab-focused objective list helps you turn knowledge into repeatable steps. You will form an LACP EtherChannel between two Catalyst switches using interface range and channel-group commands. You will configure the port-channel as a trunk and allow VLANs 10, 20, and 30. You will set the global load balance to source‑destination IP, then verify with show etherchannel summary and show interfaces port-channel 1 etherchannel. Practice confirms that identical speed, duplex, native VLAN, and trunk allowed lists are required across member interfaces. A focused troubleshooting objective teaches you how to interpret show output and identify mismatches or physical-layer problems such as an administratively down interface. Each item maps to the starter configuration provided and to checks you should run after each change. These lab objectives are built to make the configuration steps second nature and to reduce the chance of a misconfiguration causing a production outage.

EtherChannel is a method of bundling multiple physical Ethernet links into one logical interface. This logical interface is often named a Port-channel. The primary benefits are twofold. First, aggregate bandwidth: several 1‑gigabit links appear as a single higher‑capacity link, which increases throughput without requiring changes to upper-layer protocols. Second, link redundancy: if a single physical member fails, the port-channel remains operational using the remaining members, providing graceful degradation rather than a hard outage. A concrete example is connecting two switches with four GigabitEthernet links. When bundled, the pair behaves like one 4‑gigabit link. Traffic distribution across the members depends on the switch's hashing algorithm. A common misconception is that EtherChannel balances every flow evenly; in reality, the hashing algorithm maps flows to member links, so some flows remain on a single physical member. That is why choosing the right load‑balancing key matters. Remember that the port-channel is the object you configure for trunks, allowed VLANs, and Layer 2/3 settings; member interfaces are assigned to the channel-group and inherit the port-channel configuration implicitly. Consider how bundling affects failure domains and capacity planning before deployment.

There are two main dynamic negotiation protocols for EtherChannel on Cisco gear: PAgP and LACP. PAgP is Cisco‑proprietary and uses modes named desirable and auto. Desirable actively tries to form an EtherChannel, while auto waits to be contacted. LACP is an open standard (IEEE 802.3ad) and uses active and passive modes that behave similarly: active initiates negotiation and passive waits. For either protocol, one side must actively initiate for the bundle to form. A common mistake is setting both sides to the passive equivalent—auto on PAgP or passive on LACP—which prevents negotiation and leaves member interfaces unbundled. LACP is preferred in mixed‑vendor environments because it is standard, and it provides richer fault detection and negotiation. A static or forced EtherChannel using on mode bypasses negotiation altogether; this can work but removes dynamic checks and makes the setup fragile to mismatch. In practice choose LACP for interoperability and operational visibility, avoid static on in production unless you have a controlled environment, and always confirm mode pairings when a bundle fails to form. PAgP versus LACP means lacp is the open standard preferred for interoperability; pagp is cisco proprietary. mode pairing must include an active/desirable side to form a channel.. Configuring EtherChannel on Cisco Catalyst switches follows a predictable sequence. First, ensure all physical interfaces you will bundle share the same fundamental settings: speed, duplex, native VLAN, trunk encapsulation, allowed VLAN list for trunks, and Layer 2 or Layer 3 mode. Mismatches in any of those commonly prevent the bundle from forming. Next, create or use a port-channel logical interface and apply the shared configuration there. Then, assign member interfaces to the channel-group with a number and mode. For example, using LACP active mode, you run interface range GigabitEthernet1/0/1 - 4 and then channel-group 1 mode active. After grouping, the port-channel interface should reflect the common configuration. If you are creating a trunk EtherChannel, apply switchport mode trunk and switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30 on interface Port-channel1. Finally, bring interfaces up with no shutdown.
